Currently, Tesla’s Robotaxi service operates in six U.S. metropolitan areas, but the coverage is limited. For example, in Miami, the service is confined to West Miami and parts of Doral and Sweetwater. Similar small geofences exist in Orlando and Tampa. These zones typically involve low-speed routes and avoid highways and more complex urban areas.

The fleet size is also modest. Tesla reported nearly 2 million cumulative unsupervised miles by the end of Q3 2026, but third-party tracking indicates only a small number of fully driverless vehicles are on the road. This contrasts with Waymo, which has already established a presence in Orlando and Tampa and has logged over 3 million miles.

The shift in Tesla’s approach has raised concerns among investors and customers. The original pitch for FSD was a car that could eventually drive itself anywhere through a software update. However, the current plan significantly narrows the scope, focusing on fleet operations within controlled zones. This change has been described as a major shift in expectations, with critics noting that Tesla has a history of missing deadlines for FSD.

The California DMV remains a key hurdle for Tesla’s autonomous ambitions. While Tesla has a permit for testing with a driver, it has not yet received approval for driverless deployment. This delay highlights the challenges Tesla faces in meeting regulatory requirements and achieving full autonomy.

news.title: Tesla energy revenue drops 16% amid tariff-related refunds
news.summary: Tesla's energy business saw a 16% drop in revenue for Q3 2026, attributed to tariff-related customer refunds.
news.body:
Tesla’s energy business deployed more batteries in Q3 2026 but reported a 16% year-over-year decline in energy generation and storage revenue, falling to $2.88 billion. Despite a 10% increase in storage deployments to 13.7 GWh, the company cited tariff-related customer refunds as a partial reason for the drop in revenue. The exact amount refunded or the affected customers were not specified in Tesla’s shareholder letter.

The energy segment’s gross margin improved to 33.1% from 20.4% in Q2 2026, but energy gross profit still declined to $954 million from $1.07 billion in the same period a year ago. Tesla listed “lower Energy Generation and Storage gross profit” as one of the reasons for its 56% drop in operating income.

Year-to-date, Tesla has deployed 36 GWh of energy storage, up 11% from the same period in 2025. However, energy revenue is down 6% to $8.43 billion. Deployments also fell short of the 15.9 GWh that analysts had expected for Q3.

Tariffs have been a recurring factor in Tesla’s energy segment this year. In Q1 2026, Tesla noted “energy one-time benefits related to tariffs” as a driver of profit improvement. Now, the company is reportedly refunding customers, likely due to the Supreme Court’s February ruling that struck down the IEEPA tariffs. Tesla did not quantify the impact of these refunds.

Tesla is also working to reduce tariffs in its supply chain. The Texas Megafactory has begun production with 50 GWh of planned capacity, alongside 40 GWh in California and 20 GWh in Shanghai. The company also shipped its first Megapacks built entirely with its own LFP cells from Nevada, where it has 7 GWh of cell capacity in early ramp.

Storage demand remains at an “all-time high,” driven by data centers requiring faster power delivery than the grid can provide. xAI, now part of SpaceX, has purchased an additional $269 million in Megapacks this year, following $430 million in purchases in 2025.

news.title: Tesla FSD subscriptions reach 1.74 million, tied to Musk's pay package
news.summary: Tesla reports 1.74 million active Full Self-Driving subscriptions, a key metric for Elon Musk's 2025 pay package, though the count includes both upfront and monthly payments.
news.body:
Tesla has reported 1.74 million active Full Self-Driving (FSD) subscriptions, marking a 67% increase from the previous year. This figure is significant as it aligns with the metrics outlined in Elon Musk's 2025 CEO Performance Award. The count includes both upfront payments and monthly subscriptions, meaning owners who purchased FSD outright, even years ago, are counted as subscribers.

Tesla stopped selling FSD as a one-time purchase on February 14, 2026. New customers can only acquire FSD through a monthly subscription, priced at $99 in the US. However, those who paid upfront before this date, with prices reaching up to $15,000, remain in the count as long as their vehicles are active. Free trials are the only exception.

The company has not disclosed how many of the 1.74 million subscribers are currently paying the monthly fee. This lack of transparency has raised questions about the true momentum of the FSD subscription model. Tesla also reported that more than 75% of new deliveries in North America included FSD subscriptions in Q3, a significant increase from previous quarters.

Musk's 2025 pay package includes 12 tranches, each requiring specific market cap and operational milestones. As of June 30, Tesla considered only one of these milestones—20 million vehicle deliveries—as probable. The company added 260,000 net FSD subscriptions in Q3, its best quarter yet, but at the current pace, reaching 10 million active subscriptions would take several years.

Critics argue that counting upfront buyers as subscribers may inflate the metric, especially since many of these users have not yet received the promised unsupervised self-driving features. Tesla's board defined the metric, and Musk's compensation depends on it, yet the company has not provided detailed retention data for the subscription model.

news.title: Tesla cites battery supply as reason for flat sales, but prices continue to drop
news.summary: Tesla attributes flat vehicle sales to battery supply constraints, but its prices are still declining, raising questions about the true cause of the slowdown.
news.body:
Tesla has stated that battery supply, rather than demand, is the primary factor limiting its vehicle sales. In its Q3 2026 shareholder letter, the company noted that battery availability remained a key constraint on increasing production volumes during the quarter. The letter also mentioned that Tesla ended the quarter with the largest backlog for its passenger vehicles in four years, though it did not quantify the backlog.

Tesla reported record deliveries in several international markets, including Canada, Australia, Japan, and Taiwan, as well as record production at its Gigafactory Berlin. However, overall vehicle deliveries in Q3 fell by 2% compared to the same period in 2025, with Model 3 and Model Y deliveries declining by 1%. Deliveries of other models, including the Cybertruck, Semi, and remaining Model S and X units, dropped by 48%.

Tesla produced 464,391 vehicles in Q3, delivering 22,141 more than it produced, marking the second consecutive quarter of inventory reduction. Global inventory levels fell to 11 days of supply, down from 27 days in Q1 and 15 days in Q2. Despite this, Tesla cited lower average selling prices (ASP) as a factor in its revenue growth, which is unusual for a company facing supply constraints.

The company is expanding its battery cell production to support new projects like the Cybercab and Tesla Semi, as well as increased Model Y production. However, the letter also noted that Tesla is prioritizing allocation decisions between selling vehicles and using battery cells for its owned and operated fleet, which may be contributing to the supply challenges.

Critics argue that Tesla's explanation does not fully align with its financial performance, as falling prices and declining deliveries suggest a different issue may be at play. While battery supply is a real challenge, the company's strategy of directing resources toward higher-margin ventures may also be influencing its current sales trajectory.

news.title: Tesla starts Optimus production in Fremont
news.summary: Tesla has begun building production-quality Optimus humanoid robots at its Fremont, California factory.
news.body:
Tesla has started producing its Optimus humanoid robot at the Fremont factory in California, in space that previously built electric vehicles. The company announced the milestone in its third-quarter shareholder letter.

Tesla called the robots now coming off the line the first production-quality units it has made, and said the process has proven suitable for a commercial product, although it will keep refining both hardware and manufacturing.

On the earnings call, Elon Musk described the effort as early. He said Tesla is making good progress on the AI that controls the robots but that a lot of work remains before Optimus is truly useful for open-ended tasks. He expects current challenges in electromechanical design, reliability, run time and AI to be solved around the end of next year.

The spending behind Optimus and other AI projects weighed on Tesla's profit in the quarter, with research and development costs and capital expenditure both rising sharply year over year.

news.title: Tesla Q3 2026: revenue flat at $28.0 billion, profit down sharply
news.summary: Tesla beat estimates with $28.05 billion in revenue and 48 cents adjusted EPS, but GAAP net income fell to $787 million as AI spending surged.
news.body:
Tesla reported third-quarter revenue of $28.05 billion, roughly flat year over year and slightly ahead of analyst expectations. Adjusted earnings per share came in at 48 cents, beating the consensus estimate of 43 cents, according to LSEG data cited by CNBC.

GAAP net income attributable to shareholders fell to $787 million, or 22 cents per diluted share, from $1.37 billion a year earlier. Tesla blamed lower average selling prices and battery supply constraints that limited how many cars it could build against its order backlog.

## Where the money came from

Automotive revenue slipped 3% to $20.56 billion and energy generation and storage revenue fell 16% to $2.88 billion, partly because of tariff-related customer refunds. Services and other revenue rose 33% to $4.61 billion, helped by more Full Self-Driving subscriptions.

Spending climbed as Tesla invests in Optimus and other AI projects. Operating expenses rose 39% and income from operations fell to $718 million. Free cash flow was $1.53 billion, down 62% from a year ago but positive again after a negative second quarter. The shares slipped in after-hours trading.

news.title: SpaceX and Tesla boards set up committees to study a merger
news.summary: Both companies have formed special committees of independent directors to review a possible combination, Elon Musk said on SpaceX's earnings call.
news.body:
The boards of SpaceX and Tesla have each created special committees of independent directors to look at a possible merger, Elon Musk said during SpaceX's third-quarter earnings call on October 20. He said the committees were formed at the request of shareholders.

Musk, the CEO and largest individual shareholder of both companies, said he cannot take part because he is a conflicted party, and described the process as two groups talking without him in the room. He did not name the committee members.

Musk said he supports the idea, arguing there is a lot to gain from combining work on AI software, robotics, SpaceX's orbital AI data centre project Starmind and Terafab, the joint chip manufacturing effort between the two companies. But he warned that people who treat a deal as certain are overstating it, and said the committees have not agreed any terms.

Approval would be easier at SpaceX, where Musk holds more than half of the voting power since the IPO. At Tesla, a merger would need the backing of a majority of all shares outstanding.

news.title: SpaceX Q3 2026: revenue up 161% to $14.6 billion, net income $4.4 billion
news.summary: SpaceX's quarterly revenue jumped 161% year over year, driven by its Super Intelligence segment and Starlink growth, and it swung to a $4.4 billion profit.
news.body:
SpaceX (Nasdaq: SPCX) reported third-quarter revenue of $14.58 billion, up 161% from $5.58 billion a year earlier. Net income was $4.40 billion, compared with a $1.05 billion loss in the same quarter last year, and adjusted EBITDA reached $8.81 billion.

## Segment by segment

The Super Intelligence (SI) segment, which includes Grok, Grok Bot and the recently acquired Cursor, brought in $7.56 billion, up 830% year over year. Cursor, acquired on August 14, contributed $608 million. Nameplate compute reached 1.7 gigawatts at the end of September as the Colossus II build-out continued.

Connectivity, mainly Starlink, grew 69% to $5.25 billion, with operating income of $2.37 billion. Starlink ended the quarter with 13.6 million consumer subscribers, up 1.6 million in three months, and is installed on more than 3,800 aircraft.

The Space segment generated $1.77 billion from 35 launches, including the first orbital, revenue-earning Starship flight, which deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites.

Capital expenditure was $19.6 billion in the quarter, most of it on SI infrastructure. SpaceX ended September with $51.3 billion in cash plus $38.6 billion in marketable securities.

news.title: Falcon 9 launches Bandwagon-5 rideshare mission from Florida
news.summary: A Falcon 9 rocket successfully launched the Bandwagon-5 rideshare mission from Florida, carrying multiple payloads into orbit.
news.body: A Falcon 9 rocket launched successfully from Florida's Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, carrying the Bandwagon-5 rideshare mission. The mission included multiple small satellite payloads for various customers, continuing SpaceX's role in providing cost-effective access to space. The launch marked another step in SpaceX's ongoing efforts to support a diverse range of commercial and scientific missions through its rideshare program. The Falcon 9 first stage returned to Earth for a landing at the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, demonstrating the rocket's reusability and reliability. This mission was part of SpaceX's broader strategy to increase the frequency of launches and reduce the cost of orbital access for smaller satellite operators. The Bandwagon-5 mission highlights the growing demand for rideshare opportunities in the commercial space industry. SpaceX has been actively expanding its fleet of rockets and launch sites to meet the increasing demand for satellite deployment. The success of this mission further solidifies SpaceX's position as a leading provider of launch services for both government and private sector clients. The company continues to push the boundaries of space exploration and commercialization through its innovative approach to rocket design and operations.

news.title: Tesla Roadster 2.0 delays raise questions about EV innovation timeline
news.summary: Despite recent advancements in electric vehicle technology, Tesla's Roadster 2.0 remains delayed, prompting discussions about the company's progress in the EV market.
news.body:
The long-awaited Tesla Roadster 2.0 continues to face delays, leaving buyers in limbo nearly a decade after its initial announcement. While competitors have begun offering flying, self-driving, and high-performance electric vehicles, Tesla has yet to deliver on its promises for the Roadster 2.0. This has sparked conversations about the pace of innovation in the electric vehicle industry and Tesla's position within it.

Recent developments show that other companies are already delivering on advanced EV features, such as flying capabilities and self-driving technology. For example, McMurtry has begun production of its $1.36 million electric fan car, while DeLorean is reportedly working on a flying car that could hit the market before Tesla. These advancements highlight the competitive landscape Tesla now faces in the EV sector.

Some critics have pointed to Elon Musk's personal habits and focus as potential factors in the delays. However, Tesla has not officially commented on these claims. The company continues to work on its roadmap, but the absence of a concrete timeline for the Roadster 2.0 has left many consumers and industry observers questioning the company's commitment to innovation in this area.

As the EV market evolves rapidly, Tesla's ability to meet its promises will be crucial in maintaining its leadership position. The Roadster 2.0 remains a symbol of the company's vision for the future of transportation, but its continued delay may signal challenges in executing on that vision.

news.title: Starship Flight 15 and 16 milestones take shape
news.summary: SpaceX is targeting November for Flight 15, with booster and ship catch attempts, and December for Flight 16, possibly the first Starship launch from Florida.
news.body:
SpaceX is working through preparations for its last two planned Starship flights of 2026, NASASpaceFlight reports.

Flight 15 is targeted for November and aims to catch both the Super Heavy booster and the Starship upper stage with the launch tower. A ship catch would be a first and a major step toward full reusability.

Flight 16 is aimed at December and could become the first Starship launch from Launch Complex 39A at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, opening a second launch site beyond Starbase in Texas. FAA planning documents shown at an industry conference list November 8 and December 10 as tentative dates for the two flights, though these are likely to move.

If both fly, SpaceX would end the year with five Starship launches in 2026. The relatively low number reflects the switch from Block 2 to the larger Block 3 vehicles, while SpaceX continues to plan for hundreds of launches a year from Starbase in the long term.

news.title: Tesla Unveils New Roadster with Flying Features in Electrek Podcast
news.summary: Tesla unveiled a new Roadster with flying capabilities during a recent Electrek Podcast, sparking discussion about its feasibility and regulatory requirements.
news.body:
Tesla has unveiled a new version of its Roadster, featuring flying capabilities, during a recent episode of the Electrek Podcast. The discussion centered around the potential of the flying Roadster and whether its claims are realistic or exaggerated. The podcast also covered other topics related to sustainable transport and energy, including updates on Tesla’s Autopilot system and other electric vehicle developments.

The new Roadster, described as 'Cyberfied,' includes features such as the ability to kickflip, according to the articles to be discussed during the episode. However, the feasibility of the flying Roadster remains a topic of debate, with some questioning whether it is based on real technology or just 'cold gas' hype.

One top comment from listener Rob Barros suggested that if the flying Roadster ever reaches production, it should not be allowed to operate in the same airspace as ground-based transportation. He also emphasized the need for FAA licensure for such vehicles. This highlights the potential regulatory challenges that Tesla may face with its new flying Roadster.

The podcast is live every Friday at 4 p.m. ET on Electrek’s YouTube channel, with an accompanying post on the site. After the show, the video is archived on YouTube, and the audio is available on popular podcast apps. Electrek also announced a Patreon to help support the show and reduce ads.

Other topics discussed during the episode included Tesla’s Autopilot system, which was engaged when a car crossed a median and killed a man. The podcast also covered updates on the Smart #2 electric vehicle, Rivian’s Mind Robotics, and Volkswagen’s new ID. Buzz.

news.title: Tesla driver asleep with FSD engaged hits CHP car, injuring two officers
news.summary: A Tesla driver reportedly fell asleep with Full Self-Driving engaged, leading to a collision with a California Highway Patrol car at a crash scene, injuring two officers.
news.body:
Two California Highway Patrol officers were seriously injured after a Tesla struck their patrol car at a crash scene on Interstate 80 in Fairfield. The 22-year-old driver told investigators he was asleep with Tesla’s Full Self-Driving (FSD) system engaged at the time of the collision. The incident occurred just before midnight on October 13, with four lanes of traffic already closed due to flares and cones from a prior fatal crash involving a Honda Civic and a Chevrolet Tahoe.

The Tesla, traveling at highway speed, passed through the closure and collided with the Dodge Charger patrol car. The driver sustained only minor injuries, while the officers are recovering from serious injuries. The California Highway Patrol emphasized that FSD is a driver-assistance feature and does not absolve drivers of their responsibility to remain alert and in control of the vehicle. The model and software version of the Tesla involved have not yet been disclosed, and the investigation is ongoing.

This is not the first incident involving Tesla vehicles and emergency scenes. In 2021, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) launched an investigation after a series of Tesla crashes into stopped emergency vehicles. Tesla later recalled over 2 million vehicles in December 2023 to address driver-attention alerts. Despite these measures, incidents continue, including a 2024 crash involving a Tesla on FSD that hit a parked police car while officers were responding to another fatal crash.

The FSD system uses a cabin camera to monitor the driver and is designed to disengage if the driver is not paying attention. However, reports suggest that drivers can easily bypass the monitoring system, even with simple objects like a dollar bill placed in front of the camera. Elon Musk has previously stated that FSD drivers can text while driving, depending on traffic conditions, despite California laws prohibiting texting while driving.

The incident has reignited concerns about the safety of Tesla’s autonomous driving features. Critics argue that Tesla has a legal responsibility to ensure its systems can detect sleeping drivers and prevent such accidents. With multiple lawsuits and regulatory scrutiny, the company faces increasing pressure to improve the safety and reliability of its driver-assist technologies.

news.title: Tesla's New Roadster Demonstrates Impressive, But Questionable, Capabilities
news.summary: Tesla has demonstrated its next-gen Roadster with capabilities like flying and driving upside down, but questions remain about the practicality and realism of these features.
news.body:
Tesla has finally re-unveiled its next-generation Roadster, a vehicle first introduced in 2017. The car was originally intended to outperform gasoline-powered vehicles in terms of speed and performance. However, nearly a decade has passed since its initial unveiling, and Tesla has not yet released the vehicle to the public. In the meantime, several other companies have launched their own electric sports cars and set impressive records in the process.

The new Roadster was showcased with a series of impressive demonstrations, including the ability to drive upside down, fly, and accelerate from 0 to 60 mph in under one second. These feats were achieved using a combination of a 'multi-mode suction system' and 'cold gas thrusters.' The suction system, which Tesla calls a 'fan car' system, creates a low-pressure zone underneath the vehicle, allowing it to stick to surfaces and even drive upside down.

The system uses fans that generate significant downforce, though some experts question the realism of the numbers claimed by Tesla. The downforce figures appear unusually high for a vehicle of its size, and the practicality of such performance remains under scrutiny. Additionally, the use of cold gas thrusters for stunts like flying and kickflips adds complexity and mass to the vehicle, which could potentially hinder performance.

While the demonstrations were visually impressive, the practical benefits of these features for everyday driving are questionable. The 'cold gas thrusters' used for stunts like flying do not contribute to the vehicle's performance on the road. Instead, they add weight and complexity, which could negatively impact acceleration and overall efficiency. However, the side thrusters may offer some benefit in terms of cornering capability by providing additional lateral acceleration.

Tesla's CEO, Elon Musk, has long been known for making bold claims about the company's products. While the Roadster's capabilities are undeniably impressive, the question remains whether these features will translate into real-world performance or remain as marketing gimmicks.

news.title: Tesla unveils thruster-equipped Roadster, due in 2028
news.summary: Tesla revealed the second-generation Roadster near Waco, Texas, with SpaceX-style cold-gas thrusters and three trims, and said it will build the car in 2028.
news.body:
Tesla showed off its long-delayed second-generation Roadster at an event outside Waco, Texas. In a demonstration, the car used fans and cold-gas thrusters to drive up an inverted ramp, spin around and lift itself over other Tesla vehicles before landing.

Elon Musk said production will start in 2028 but did not give a price. Tesla is offering three trims. Performance seats two and is described as road-ready, with active aerodynamics and a suction system for grip. Thrust adds rear thrusters that Tesla says deliver 0 to 60 mph in under one second. Rocket is a single-seater with 10 thrusters and is invite-only.

All three trims are rated for about 300 miles of range and top speeds above 230 mph. Reservations opened on Tesla's website at $50,000 for Performance and $250,000 for Thrust.

Engineering vice president Lars Moravy said the thrusters run on 600 litres of compressed air stored in carbon-fibre pressure vessels packed into every usable space in the car, and the tank can be recharged.

news.title: Tesla Robotaxi crashes linked to remote operators, data reveals
news.summary: Tesla's Robotaxi service has seen five crashes involving remote operators taking control, all resulting in collisions, according to recent federal data.
news.body:
Tesla’s latest crash reports to federal regulators reveal that two additional Robotaxi incidents involved remote operators taking control of the vehicle, leading to collisions. This brings the total number of such crashes to five, with every remote takeover resulting in a collision.

Both new incidents occurred in August and were included in the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s (NHTSA) September release of Standing General Order data. Tesla now has 36 unique Robotaxi incident reports, up from 22 in July. In one case, a Model Y was stopped on a residential street, wedged between a concrete mixer truck and a parked SUV. A remote operator took control and the vehicle made contact with the SUV at approximately 0.40 mph. No passengers were aboard.

In another incident in Austin, a remote operator was in control of a Model Y navigating an alley. The vehicle hit a dumpster at about 1 mph. Both incidents involved property damage only and were at walking speeds. Tesla’s structured code for the Driver/Operator Type in both cases was labeled “Remote (Commercial / Test).”

The pattern of crashes follows a similar script: the autonomous system gets stuck or needs assistance, a human takes over remotely, and the human causes a collision. Tesla has not disclosed how often remote operators intervene, making it impossible to calculate a rate. However, all five known remote takeovers have resulted in contact.

Waymo, Tesla’s main robotaxi competitor, has a different approach. In a February 2026 letter to Senator Ed Markey, Waymo stated it does not use remote driving where a human performs the Dynamic Driving Task. Instead, remote staff provide guidance that the vehicle can accept or reject. Waymo has one narrow exception, allowing a trained agent to nudge a stuck vehicle forward at 2 mph with fixed steering angles, but this has never been used on public roads.

The data highlights the risks associated with remote teleoperation, including latency and limited situational awareness for the operator. Experts suggest that giving riders a control stick or providing supplemental guidance to the onboard system may be safer alternatives.

news.title: Tesla confirms Autopilot/FSD was engaged in fatal median crossing crash
news.summary: Tesla confirmed its driver-assist system was engaged when a car crossed a median and killed a man in New Jersey.
news.body:
A Tesla Model Y crossed the grass median of Route 55 in New Jersey, hit a tree, and slid into oncoming traffic, striking an SUV head-on. The SUV's driver, 68-year-old Phillip Eastman, was killed. New Jersey State Police reported the incident as a case of a driver losing control, but Tesla's report to federal regulators indicated that the car's driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of the crash.

The incident occurred around 8:31 a.m. on August 22, 2026, near milepost 34.6 on Route 55 in Vineland, Cumberland County. The Tesla's driver and a passenger in the Chevrolet SUV were injured and taken to the hospital with moderate injuries. Eastman, who had recently been sworn in as a Springfield School District board member and had a long history coaching ice hockey, was widely mourned in the Philadelphia area.

Tesla filed a report with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), identifying the vehicle as a 2021 Model Y and marking the automation as 'Verified Engaged.' However, Tesla redacted key details, including the crash narrative, software version, and whether the road was within the system's approved operating area, labeling them as 'confidential business information.'

The data does not confirm whether the driver was overriding the system or whether the software was basic Autopilot or Full Self-Driving (FSD). Tesla also logged a pre-crash speed of 37 mph, which is lower than typical freeway speeds, and only holds the car's telematics, not the event-data recorder or video.

Tesla is currently under NHTSA investigation over its reporting practices. The incident highlights concerns about the transparency of driver-assist systems and the potential risks of misinterpreting Level 2 automation as full autonomy. The public and investigators are calling for full disclosure of the data to understand the circumstances of the crash.

Electrek is continuing its investigation to match reported crashes with Tesla's NHTSA filings, emphasizing the need for transparency in how driver-assist systems operate and the data they collect.

news.title: Grok Voice 3.0 launches with top speech-to-speech scores
news.summary: SpaceX's AI unit released Grok Voice 3.0, which ranks first on Artificial Analysis' speech-to-speech index, at the same API price as before.
news.body:
SpaceX Super Intelligence, the AI business formerly known as xAI, has released Grok Voice 3.0, a speech-to-speech model it calls the most intelligent voice model available.

In independent testing by Artificial Analysis, the model scored 86.9 on the Speech-to-Speech Index, ahead of rival models from OpenAI and Google, and 97% on Full Duplex Bench, which measures how naturally it handles pauses and interruptions. Response latency is under one second.

## Already in heavy use

The company says Grok Voice handles millions of conversations a day in Tesla vehicles, where drivers can ask it to check calendars, answer email or hand bigger jobs to Grok Bot. Starlink's call centres use it to answer around 20,000 customer calls a day in several languages, with roughly 70% resolved without a human.

Grok Voice 3.0 is available now in the API at $0.08 per minute, unchanged from version 2.0. Apps already pointing to the latest model were switched over automatically.

news.title: SpaceXSI bundles Grok, Grok Bot, Cursor and X Premium into one plan
news.summary: The X Subscription combines SpaceX's AI and social products in tiers from free to $200 a month, with shared AI usage across Grok and Cursor.
news.body:
SpaceX Super Intelligence has launched The X Subscription, a single plan that bundles Grok, Grok Bot, the Cursor coding tools and X Premium.

There are five tiers: Free, Plus at $8 a month, Premium at $30, Super at $100 and Ultra at $200. Usage limits rise with each tier, and paid plans share a pool of Grok model usage across the Grok apps, the Grok tab on X and Cursor. The company says Premium covers what previously cost about $90 a month for SuperGrok, Cursor Pro and X Premium+ combined. Premium or higher is needed for the newest Grok models.

The bundle is available to new customers now and is rolling out gradually to existing SuperGrok, Cursor and X Premium subscribers, who can switch in their billing settings and receive a prorated refund, or keep their current plan.

The move is aimed at winning subscribers in a crowded paid-AI market where the company competes with OpenAI, Anthropic and others.

news.title: Starlink Mobile buys 800 MHz spectrum as FCC approves 15,000-satellite constellation
news.summary: SpaceX agreed to acquire nationwide 800 MHz low-band spectrum for Starlink Mobile, and the FCC authorised its next-generation 15,000-satellite direct-to-phone constellation.
news.body:
SpaceX announced two milestones for Starlink Mobile, its effort to become a full mobile carrier in the United States.

First, it agreed to acquire a nationwide portfolio of up to 14 megahertz of paired spectrum in the 800 MHz band. Low-band spectrum travels further and penetrates walls better, so it can keep phones connected indoors. SpaceX notes that most existing phones already support the band. The deal is expected to close in the first half of 2027, subject to FCC approval.

Second, the FCC approved Starlink Mobile's Gen2 constellation, authorising up to 15,000 satellites optimised for 2 GHz spectrum worldwide. SpaceX says these V2 satellites will offer more than 100 times the bandwidth of the current generation, connecting unmodified phones almost anywhere. The FCC also cleared the backhaul bands used by Starlink's V3 broadband satellites.

SpaceX plans to combine satellites and ground-based networks, which it says would make Starlink Mobile the first operator to deploy both satellite and terrestrial spectrum on one network.

news.title: Tesla delivers 486,532 vehicles in Q3 2026
news.summary: Tesla produced 464,391 vehicles and delivered 486,532 in the third quarter, and deployed 13.7 GWh of energy storage.
news.body:
Tesla delivered 486,532 vehicles in the third quarter of 2026 and produced 464,391, according to its quarterly production and deliveries report.

The Model 3 and Model Y made up the bulk of the numbers, with 478,237 deliveries and 457,387 units produced. Other models, including the Cybertruck, contributed 8,295 deliveries and 7,004 units produced. Deliveries outpacing production means Tesla drew down some of its inventory during the quarter.

The energy business deployed 13.7 gigawatt-hours of storage products such as Megapack and Powerwall.

Tesla later said in its earnings report that vehicle deliveries were lower than a year earlier and that battery supply limited how many cars it could build to meet its order backlog.

news.title: Music City Loop: two tunnel boring machines now digging in Nashville
news.summary: The Boring Company says Prufrock-MB1 and MB2 are tunnelling at the same time, MB3 launches in late October and MB4 is being built.
news.body:
The Boring Company's latest Music City Loop update says two tunnel boring machines, Prufrock-MB1 and Prufrock-MB2, are now digging at the same time in Nashville, all supported from a site of less than one acre.

A third machine, Prufrock-MB3, is set to launch in late October from a new site where the launch pit, power supply and support systems are being prepared. A fourth, MB4, is under construction, and the team aims to have four machines in the ground before the end of the year. The company says it has made more than 300 upgrades to MB1 alone, all of which carry over to later machines.

## Stations and approvals

All permits needed ahead of tunnelling have been obtained, including a Tennessee Department of Transportation permit covering 25 miles of tunnel. The airport authority and the convention centre authority have both approved connections, and more than 40 stations are in planning, including agreements with residential towers and the JW Marriott downtown.

The Music City Loop is planned to carry paying passengers in Tesla vehicles between downtown Nashville and the airport.

news.title: Neuralink trains a foundation model on 50,000 hours of brain data
news.summary: Neuralink says implant users have logged over 50,000 hours, and a model pretrained on that data cut calibration for some users from daily to weekly.
news.body:
Neuralink says participants in its clinical trials have now used their brain implants for more than 50,000 hours, creating one of the largest datasets of recorded neural activity from inside the brain.

The company used that data to pretrain what it calls a foundation model for brain-computer interfaces: self-supervised encoders that turn noisy, shifting neural signals into stable representations.

## Early results

According to Neuralink, decoders built on the model keep working for weeks instead of days. For some users, the calibration needed fell from about 10 minutes a day to 10 minutes a week. The company also showed cursors that jump directly to the intended target, and reported a new cursor-control record of 11.32 bits per second, which it says beats most able-bodied people.

Neuralink says next steps include pooling data across participants, calibration with one example or none at all, and an interface for developers to build on motor-cortex signals.
